content_voiceover: This map is the classic board image for hemoglobinopathy geography, and examiners love testing exactly which variant goes with which region. Alpha thalassemia trait and beta thalassemia intermedia cluster across Africa, the Mediterranean, India, and Eastern Europe, tracking the historical malaria belt since heterozygous carriers get relative protection from falciparum malaria. Hemoglobin H disease is most concentrated in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean, which matters because that's where the large alpha-globin deletions like the Southeast Asian deletion are common. Hemoglobin E beta thalassemia is the dominant severe hemoglobinopathy of East India, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia, and it's actually the most common form of severe thalassemia worldwide once you count hemoglobin E combined with beta thalassemia mutations. The last high-yield point is migration: prevalence in Europe and North America is rising specifically because of population movement out of these endemic zones, so a board question can absolutely present a European or American patient of appropriate ancestry with microcytic anemia and expect you to think thalassemia, not just iron deficiency.
keypoints: Malaria belt distribution: Africa, Mediterranean, India, East Europe, SE Asia
HbH disease: Southeast Asia, Middle East, Mediterranean
HbE/beta-thalassemia: East India, Bangladesh, SE Asia (most common severe thalassemia worldwide)
Migration is increasing prevalence in Europe and North America
Always factor ancestry into a microcytic anemia workup
keypoint_voiceover: Quick recap: this distribution map follows the historic malaria belt, since carrier states offer protection against falciparum malaria. Alpha thalassemia trait and beta thalassemia intermedia are widespread across Africa, the Mediterranean, India, and Eastern Europe. Hemoglobin H disease concentrates in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean. Hemoglobin E beta thalassemia, centered in East India, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia, is actually the most common severe thalassemia syndrome globally. And remember, migration means these diagnoses now show up well outside their traditional geography, so ancestry should always factor into your workup of a microcytic anemia.
